content: Infectious salmon anemia (ISA) is a viral disease that primarily affects Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and has caused significant losses in fish farms located in Canada, Norway, and Scotland. The causative agent of this disease is the infectious salmon anemia virus (ISAV), which is the sole member of the genus Isavirus within the family Orthomyxoviridae. Pathology ISA leads to severe anemia in infected fish. Affected fish often exhibit pale gills and may swim near the water's surface, gasping for air. However, the disease can also progress without any visible external symptoms. In such cases, the fish may appear healthy, maintain a normal appetite, and then die suddenly. The disease can spread gradually across an infected farm, and in severe outbreaks, mortality rates can approach 100%. Post-mortem examinations of infected fish reveal a variety of pathological changes. The liver and spleen may be swollen, congested, or show signs of necrosis. The circulatory system may fail, and the blood may contain dead blood cells. Red blood cells that remain are often fragile and prone to rupture, with an increased presence of immature and damaged blood cells. ISA shares similarities with influenza viruses in terms of its behavior and characteristics. The exact mechanisms of transmission and the natural reservoirs of ISAV remain incompletely understood. While Atlantic salmon are the primary species affected, sea-run brown trout (Salmo trutta) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) can also be infected. However, these species do not exhibit clinical signs of the disease, suggesting they may act as carriers or reservoirs for the virus. Spread of the Disease The first documented outbreak of ISA occurred in the autumn of 1984 among farmed Atlantic salmon along the southwest coast of Norway. The disease spread gradually, and by June 1988, it had become widespread enough for the Norwegian Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food to classify it as a notifiable disease. In the summer of 1996, a similar disease emerged in farmed Atlantic salmon in New Brunswick, Canada. This outbreak, characterized by high mortality rates, was initially termed hemorrhagic kidney syndrome. Subsequent research by Norwegian and Canadian scientists confirmed that the same virus was responsible for both ISA and hemorrhagic kidney syndrome. In May 1998, a suspected outbreak of ISA was reported at a salmon farm in Loch Nevis, located on the west coast of Scotland. The diagnosis was confirmed, and by the end of the year, the disease had spread to 15 additional farms, including those on the Scottish mainland, Skye, and Shetland. Transmission ISAV is transmitted through direct contact with infected fish or their secretions. The virus can also spread via contaminated equipment or individuals who have handled infected fish. ISAV is capable of surviving in seawater, making proximity to an infected farm a significant risk factor for uninfected farms. Recent studies have identified the sea louse, a small crustacean parasite that damages the protective mucous, scales, and skin of salmon, as a potential passive carrier of the virus. The virus has been detected on the surface and within the digestive tract of sea lice. However, there is no evidence to date that sea lice can actively transmit the virus or that ISAV can replicate within the sea louse. This is consistent with the general behavior of viruses, which are typically highly host-specific, unlike certain bacterial pathogens that can replicate in arthropod vectors, such as those responsible for Lyme disease or Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Control and Treatment ISA poses a significant threat to the sustainability of salmon farming and is classified as a List One disease under the European Commission’s fish health regime. This classification mandates the complete eradication of all fish stocks on a farm where an outbreak is confirmed. ISA is also considered a serious threat to declining populations of wild salmon. Anecdotal evidence suggests that fish surviving an initial infection may develop immunity to the virus. Efforts are currently underway to develop a vaccine against ISA. Preliminary findings indicate that the North American strain of ISAV may differ slightly from the Norwegian strain, suggesting that the sudden appearance of the disease in Canada was unlikely to have resulted from the importation of infected Norwegian fish. This genetic variation raises concerns that a single vaccine may only be effective within specific regions or for limited durations.
